The projection is the “shadow” of on the line through . It always lies along that line — in the direction of when the angle is acute, in the opposite direction when it is obtuse. Its length has nothing to do with how long is; only supplies the direction of the line.

Explanation (added)

A vector is “how far” times “which way”. The scalar projection is the how-far (a signed length), the unit vector is the which-way. Multiplying the two denominators gives the in the boxed form, and , so no square root is ever needed for the vector projection.

What a typical exam question looks like

Questions on this section are short computations built on the examples above:

  • “Find the angle between and ” — exact value as an inverse cosine, then to the nearest degree.
  • “Determine whether the vectors are orthogonal, parallel, or neither”, or “find the value of that makes orthogonal to ”.
  • “Find the direction cosines and direction angles of .”
  • “Find the scalar and vector projections of onto .” (Read the order carefully: of onto means goes in the denominator.)
  • “A force moves an object from point to point . Find the work done.”
  • A short proof using the properties, in the style of the expansion.
